Opposite situationActing without a license = illegal or unauthorized
One Sentence to Remember It By

A license is the official permission — granted by someone with the authority to grant it — that allows you to do something you would otherwise not be legally or rightfully allowed to do.

Everything else you read above is just the richness and variety of how that one core idea plays out across different areas of life.
9790:
Licensing is the process of granting or receiving official permission to do something, use something, or operate something — under a specific set of agreed conditions.

Think of it this way: you own something valuable (an idea, a product, a brand, a skill, or a right). You don't want to give it away permanently, but you're willing to let someone else use it — for a fee, for a limited time, or under certain rules. The activity of making that arrangement happen is called licensing.

The key insight is that licensing is about permission, not ownership. The thing being licensed still belongs to its original owner. The other party simply gets the right to use it.

Every licensing situation has two sides:

  • The licensor — the person or organization giving the permission. They own the thing being licensed.
  • The licensee — the person or organization receiving the permission. They get to use the thing, within the agreed limits.

The formal document that records their agreement is called a license agreement (or licensing agreement). It spells out what the licensee can and cannot do, how long the permission lasts, how much they must pay, and under what conditions the permission can be taken away.
Where Licensing Appears in Real Life

Licensing shows up in many different areas of life. Here are the most important ones:

1. Intellectual Property Licensing

When someone creates something original — a song, a book, an invention, a logo — they automatically own the rights to it. This is called intellectual property (IP). Licensing allows the creator to let others use their creation without giving up ownership.

  • A musician licenses their song to an advertising company to use in a commercial. The musician still owns the song; the company just has permission to use it in that specific context.
  • A pharmaceutical company invents a drug and licenses the formula to a manufacturer in another country. The manufacturer can produce and sell the drug, but the original company still owns the invention.
  • An author licenses the rights to their book to a foreign publisher, allowing it to be translated and sold in another country.

2. Software Licensing

When you buy software, you're almost never buying the software itself — you're buying a license to use it. The software company retains full ownership.

  • When you install Microsoft Word, you agree to a license that says you can use this software on your computer, but you cannot copy it, resell it, or modify it.
  • When a business subscribes to a cloud tool like Salesforce or Adobe Creative Cloud, they're paying for an ongoing license. If they stop paying, the license ends and they lose access.

This is also why software companies talk about "license keys" and "license violations" — they are managing who has permission to use their product.

3. Brand and Character Licensing

Large, recognizable brands and characters are extremely valuable. Companies often license these to others who want to use them on their products.

  • Marvel licenses its superhero characters (like Spider-Man or Iron Man) to toy manufacturers, clothing brands, and video game studios. Those companies pay Marvel for the right to use the characters.
  • Disney licenses Mickey Mouse to thousands of products worldwide. You can see this on cups, T-shirts, school bags, and theme parks in other countries — all using the character through a licensing deal.
  • A sports league like the NFL licenses team logos and names to apparel companies who then sell official merchandise.

This kind of licensing is often called brand licensing or character licensing, and it's a massive global industry worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

4. Franchise Licensing

A franchise is a specific and very common form of business licensing. When a company like McDonald's, Subway, or KFC allows an individual or business to open a branch using their name, recipes, systems, and branding — that is a licensing arrangement.

The franchise owner (the licensee) pays fees, follows strict rules set by the parent company (the licensor), and operates under the brand's name. They don't own the brand, the recipes, or the systems — they're licensed to use them.

5. Professional and Occupational Licensing

Governments use licensing to control who is allowed to practice certain professions — usually for public safety and quality assurance.

  • A doctor must obtain a medical license from a government authority before they can practice medicine. Without it, treating patients is illegal.
  • A lawyer must pass bar exams and receive a license to practice law.
  • A pilot needs a license to fly a commercial aircraft.
  • An electrician, pharmacist, or real estate agent all need specific licenses in most countries.

In this context, licensing serves as a guarantee to the public: this person has met the required standard and is officially permitted to do this work.

6. Government and Regulatory Licensing

Businesses also need licenses from governments to operate in certain industries, to sell certain products, or to perform certain activities.

  • A restaurant needs a license to sell alcohol.
  • A radio station needs a broadcasting license to transmit on a specific frequency.
  • A bank needs a license from the central bank to take deposits from customers.
  • A factory may need an environmental license to release any emissions.

These licenses exist because some activities carry risk or involve shared public resources (like airwaves), so the government decides who gets to do them and under what conditions.

Terms and Conditions

Every license comes with a set of rules — what the licensee can do and what they cannot do. For example, a license might say: "You can use this song in online videos, but not in television commercials." Or: "You can sell this product in India, but not in Pakistan." Violating these terms usually results in the license being cancelled or legal action being taken.

Royalties

A royalty is a recurring payment a licensee makes to the licensor for the right to keep using something. It's typically calculated as a percentage of sales or revenue.

For example, if a publisher licenses the right to print a novelist's book, they might pay the author a royalty of 10% on every copy sold. This means the author earns money every time a copy sells, without doing any additional work.

Duration

Most licenses are not permanent. They last for a defined period — say, five years. After that, the license must be renewed (with possible renegotiation of terms) or it expires. When a license expires without renewal, the licensee must stop using whatever was licensed.

Scope

The scope of a license defines the limits of the permission — geographically, in terms of use, in terms of volume, or in terms of medium. For instance, a license might be limited to a particular country, a particular language, or a particular platform (like streaming only, not physical sales).

Exclusive vs. Non-Exclusive Licensing

  • An exclusive license means only one licensee gets the permission. Nobody else — not even the licensor themselves — can use the thing in the same way during the license period. This is more valuable and therefore usually more expensive.
  • A non-exclusive license means the licensor can grant the same permission to many people at once. Software licenses are usually non-exclusive — millions of users can all have a license to the same software simultaneously.

Sublicensing

Sometimes a licensee is given the right to pass on their permission to others. This is called sublicensing. For example, a publisher (licensee) who has the right to publish a book might sublicense the audio rights to an audiobook company.

It's important to distinguish licensing from selling or assigning rights.

  • When you sell or assign your rights to something, you permanently transfer ownership to the buyer. You no longer have any claim over it.
  • When you license something, you keep ownership. You're only granting temporary, conditional permission to use it.

For example: if a songwriter sells a song to a music company, the company now owns the song and the songwriter has no further claim. But if the songwriter licenses it, the songwriter still owns the song — the company just has permission to use it under the agreed conditions.

Licensing is one of the most important mechanisms in modern economies because it allows valuable things — inventions, brands, ideas, creative works — to be shared and used widely without the original owner losing control or ownership. It enables:

  • Creators and inventors to earn money from their work without giving it away permanently
  • Businesses to use others' technology or brands without having to develop or create them from scratch
  • Governments to regulate dangerous or resource-intensive activities for public safety
  • Professionals to be held to a verified standard before serving the public

In short, licensing makes it possible for knowledge, creativity, and capability to flow through the economy in an organized, fair, and legally protected way.
9791:
Licentious means having no moral restraint, especially when it comes to sexual behavior or pleasure. It describes someone who freely and openly pursues desires — particularly sexual ones — in a way that goes against what society considers decent, ethical, or acceptable.

Think of it this way: "license" in everyday English means permission. A licentious person has basically given themselves unlimited personal permission to do whatever they want, throwing morality, decency, and social standards out the window.

The word does two things at once:

1. It points to a lack of restraint. A licentious person doesn't hold back. They indulge freely and excessively, without self-control.

2. It carries a moral judgment. This is important. The word doesn't just mean someone enjoys pleasure — it means they pursue it in a way that is considered wrong or shameful. It is a criticism, not a neutral description.

So if someone calls a person licentious, they are not simply saying that person is fun-loving or free-spirited. They are saying that person crosses moral and ethical lines, especially in matters of sexuality, and does so repeatedly and without shame.

While "licentious" is most commonly used to describe sexual behavior, it can occasionally stretch a little wider to describe any behavior that recklessly ignores moral rules or social laws — though this broader use is less common. In almost all real-world contexts you will encounter, however, it will be about sexual immorality or moral looseness of a sexual nature.

It can describe:

  • A person — a licentious man, a licentious ruler
  • Behavior — licentious conduct, licentious acts
  • Content — a licentious novel, licentious art
The Tone and Feel of the Word

This is a formal, literary word. You are far more likely to read it in a novel, a historical account, a news opinion piece, or a formal essay than to hear it in everyday conversation. It has a slightly old-fashioned, elevated tone, which is part of why writers use it — it carries a sense of weight and seriousness that a simpler word like "sleazy" does not.

When someone uses "licentious," they are typically making a firm moral condemnation. It is never a compliment. It signals disapproval, and often a degree of disgust.
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Promiscuous focuses specifically on having many sexual partners. Licentious is broader — it's about overall moral abandon, not just partner count.
  • Lewd focuses on offensive or crude sexual behavior or language. Licentious is more about the lifestyle or character as a whole.
  • Lascivious focuses on feeling or expressing strong, inappropriate sexual desire. Licentious focuses more on the behavior and lack of moral control that results from that desire.
  • Dissolute and debauched are the closest to licentious — they all describe someone who has abandoned moral standards in pursuit of pleasure. "Debauched" often implies that the person has been corrupted or ruined. "Licentious" puts more emphasis on the freedom-from-rules angle.

Here are some sentences that show the word in action:

  • "The king's licentious lifestyle — endless parties, affairs, and scandals — eventually turned his court against him."
  • "The book was banned in several countries for its licentious content."
  • "She was disgusted by his licentious behavior at a gathering that was meant to be professional."
  • "History often portrays the last years of the Roman Empire as an era of licentious excess."
  • "A man of licentious character, he had little regard for commitment or fidelity."

• Licentiousness (noun) — the quality or state of being licentious.

"The licentiousness of the aristocracy was a source of public outrage."

  • Licentiously (adverb) — in a licentious manner.

"He behaved licentiously throughout his youth."
A Quick Way to Remember It

Picture someone who has written themselves a blank check of permission — they can do anything they want, break any moral rule, satisfy any desire — especially sexual ones — and they feel no guilt about any of it. That person is licentious. The word is essentially saying: this person has too much license, and they are using it in morally wrong ways.
9792:
Licentiousness means behavior that is morally unrestrained, especially in a sexual way, with total disregard for rules, decency, or the rights of others.

A licentious person essentially does whatever they want — particularly in sexual matters — without any sense of limits, guilt, or respect for moral boundaries.

Think of it this way. Society has certain rules and moral codes — not just laws, but widely understood ideas about what is decent and acceptable behavior, especially around sex and personal conduct. Most people, even when they privately disagree with some of these rules, still follow them out of respect, self-discipline, or consideration for others.

A licentious person throws all of that out the window. They indulge every desire — especially sexual desire — freely, excessively, and without any moral restraint. They don't care what is right or wrong. They don't care who gets hurt. They simply do what feels good to them, with no accountability.

So licentiousness is not just casual rule-breaking. It is a pattern of deeply unrestrained, morally irresponsible behavior — and the word always carries a strong sense of disapproval and condemnation.

Licentiousness actually works on two levels, and understanding both will help you use the word precisely:

1. Sexual immorality and promiscuity (the primary meaning)
This is the most common use. Licentiousness here means engaging in sexual behavior with no moral limits whatsoever — sleeping with many people indiscriminately, pursuing lust without commitment, faithfulness, or decency. It's not just about being sexually active; it's about being sexually reckless and irresponsible in a way that offends moral standards.

Example: "The emperor was infamous for his licentiousness — he pursued every indulgence with no thought for virtue or fidelity."

2. General lawlessness and moral disorder (the broader meaning)
Sometimes the word is used beyond the sexual realm to describe behavior that is simply out of control and without any moral or legal restraint — a reckless disregard for all rules and norms, not just sexual ones.

Example: "The festival descended into licentiousness — people were stealing, fighting, and causing chaos with complete abandon."

In most real-world usage, the first meaning (sexual) is dominant. But the second meaning is always lurking underneath, because the idea of "no moral limits whatsoever" is at the heart of the word either way.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

Several words sound similar to licentiousness, but each has its own flavor:

  • Promiscuity is specifically about having many casual sexual partners. It's a narrower, more clinical word. Licentiousness is broader and carries more moral weight — it implies not just many partners, but a complete collapse of moral values.
  • Debauchery is very close to licentiousness and is often used interchangeably. Debauchery emphasizes excessive indulgence — in drink, sex, and wild pleasure. Licentiousness puts more emphasis on the absence of moral restraint rather than just the excess.
  • Lasciviousness is about openly displaying or expressing sexual desire in a way that is offensive or inappropriate. It is about the attitude and expression. Licentiousness is about the full pattern of behavior.
  • Wantonness means acting in a deliberately reckless, uncaring way — often sexually, but also in other ways. It emphasizes the carelessness and lack of concern for consequences or others. Licentiousness is very similar but places greater stress on the moral dimension.
  • Depravity is a stronger, darker word meaning deep moral corruption. Someone who is depraved has reached a very low moral state overall. Licentiousness is more focused on unbridled indulgence; depravity implies a deeper moral rottenness.

This is an important point. Licentiousness is never a neutral word. It is always used as a criticism — often a sharp, serious, or even old-fashioned moral condemnation. When someone accuses a person, a society, or an era of licentiousness, they are expressing strong moral disapproval.

You will often see it used in:

  • Religious or moral writing (sermons, philosophical texts, ethical arguments)
  • Historical descriptions of decadent societies or rulers
  • Literary criticism or analysis of characters who are morally corrupt
  • Formal or elevated writing where precise moral language is called for

You would not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation — it has a formal, somewhat literary feel.

To make the meaning even clearer, consider its opposites:

  • Chastity — purity, especially sexual restraint
  • Virtue — moral goodness and right conduct
  • Decency — behavior that follows accepted social and moral standards
  • Self-restraint — controlling one's desires and impulses
  • Propriety — correct and proper behavior according to social norms

Here are varied examples to show you how the word functions in real sentences:

  1. "Historians have long debated whether the licentiousness of Rome's ruling class contributed to the empire's eventual collapse."
  2. "The preacher warned his congregation against the licentiousness he saw spreading through the city's culture."
  3. "Her novel explored the licentiousness of the aristocracy — the endless affairs, the broken promises, the moral emptiness beneath the gilded surface."
  4. "He mistook licentiousness for freedom, not realizing that true freedom requires self-discipline and respect for others."
  5. "The court was scandalized by the licentiousness of the young prince."

If you want to lock the meaning in your memory forever, remember this:

Licentiousness is the total abandonment of moral restraint — especially in sexual behavior — with no concern for rules, decency, or the impact on others, and it is always used as a strong moral criticism.
9793:
A lichen is not a single living thing. It is two (sometimes three) completely different organisms living together so intimately that they look and function as one. Think of it as a biological partnership — a tiny, self-contained community packaged into what appears to be a single body.

The two partners are:

  • A fungus (the main structural partner)
  • A photosynthetic partner — usually a green alga, a cyanobacterium, or both

Neither partner could survive as well alone in the harsh places where lichens thrive. Together, they form something entirely new — so new, in fact, that scientists give the combined organism its own name, its own species classification, and treat it as a distinct living entity.

The fungus builds the body of the lichen. It forms a protective outer shell and a spongy internal network that physically holds everything together. It absorbs water and minerals from rain and the surrounding surface. It anchors the lichen to rock, bark, or soil. Essentially, the fungus provides the house.

The alga or cyanobacterium lives safely inside that house and does the cooking. Using sunlight, it performs photosynthesis — producing sugars and organic compounds that feed both partners. Without this, the fungus would have no food source.

In return, the alga gets protection from drying out, from harsh UV radiation, and from being washed away. The fungus, quite literally, gives the alga a home in places that would otherwise be uninhabitable.

Some lichens have a third partner — a cyanobacterium alongside a green alga — which adds the bonus of being able to "fix" nitrogen from the air, converting it into a form that living things can use.

Lichens come in a surprising range of shapes, textures, and colors — grays, greens, yellows, oranges, reds, and even black. Broadly, they grow in three main forms:

Crustose lichens look like a thin crust or paint splattered directly onto a surface. They are so tightly fused to the rock or bark underneath that you cannot peel them off without destroying them. You have almost certainly seen these as crusty gray, green, or orange patches on old stone walls, gravestones, or pavement.

Foliose lichens are flat and leaf-like, with lobes that curl up slightly at the edges. They are loosely attached to their surface and can sometimes be peeled off in one piece. They look a little like crinkled, flattened leaves lying on bark or rock.

Fruticose lichens are the most three-dimensional. They grow upright like tiny shrubs, or hang downward like hair or tangled threads from tree branches. The "old man's beard" you might see dangling from forest trees is a fruticose lichen.

Lichens are famous for colonizing places where almost nothing else can live:

  • Bare rock faces — cliff sides, boulders, mountain tops
  • Tree bark — they are common on the outer bark of trees, though they do not harm the tree
  • Soil — especially in deserts and arctic regions, where they form a thin biological crust
  • Old walls, gravestones, roof tiles, fence posts
  • Antarctic ice-free rock — some lichens survive in one of the most hostile environments on Earth

Because they are often the very first living things to appear on a bare, lifeless rock surface, lichens are called pioneer species. Over long periods of time, they chemically and physically break down rock surfaces, slowly beginning the process of soil formation that eventually allows plants to grow.
How Slowly They Grow — and How Long They Live

Lichens are among the slowest-growing organisms on Earth. Many species grow less than a millimeter per year. A lichen patch the size of your palm on a rock might be decades — or even centuries — old.

Some of the oldest living organisms on the planet are lichens. Certain Arctic and Antarctic lichens are estimated to be thousands of years old, potentially making them older than most trees, older than many civilizations.

Because their growth rate is so predictable, scientists use the size of lichen patches on rocks to estimate how long a surface has been exposed — a technique called lichenometry. It has been used to date ancient moraines (rock deposits left by glaciers) and even archaeological structures.

Lichens reproduce in a few ways:

Vegetative reproduction — small fragments of the lichen break off (through wind, rain, or animals brushing past) and land somewhere new. If conditions are right, each fragment can grow into a new lichen.

Soredia and isidia — many lichens produce tiny powdery granules called soredia (or peg-like outgrowths called isidia) that contain both the fungal threads and the algal cells together, ready to start a new lichen wherever they land.

Sexual reproduction — the fungal partner can produce spores through cup-like or disc-like structures on the lichen's surface. However, these spores contain only the fungal partner. For a new lichen to form, the germinating spore must encounter and "recruit" the right type of alga or cyanobacterium — a process that is uncertain and not always successful.

In ecosystems:

  • They are critical food sources in extreme environments. Reindeer and caribou rely heavily on ground-dwelling lichens (often called "reindeer moss," though that name is misleading — it is a lichen) during Arctic winters when nothing else is available.
  • They provide nesting material for birds and shelter for tiny insects and mites.
  • Nitrogen-fixing lichens enrich soils, making them more fertile for other life.
  • They play a key role in breaking down rock into soil over geological timescales.

As environmental indicators:
Lichens are extraordinarily sensitive to air pollution, especially sulfur dioxide and other pollutants. They absorb water and dissolved chemicals directly from the air with no filtering mechanism. In heavily polluted urban areas, most lichens vanish. Scientists use the presence, absence, and health of lichen species as a reliable indicator of air quality — a practice called bioindication. The diversity of lichens in an area is a direct measure of how clean the air is.

For humans:

  • Certain lichens have been used historically as natural dyes — the vivid purple-red dye orchil (or archil) was extracted from lichens and used to color cloth for centuries, including in ancient Mediterranean cultures.
  • Some lichens have antibiotic properties. Usnea (a hanging, hair-like lichen) contains usnic acid, which has antimicrobial effects and has been used in traditional medicine and in some modern topical preparations.
  • Some indigenous peoples have used certain lichens as food in times of scarcity, though raw lichens often contain bitter or mildly toxic acids and must be prepared carefully.
  • Litmus paper — used in chemistry to test whether a solution is acidic or alkaline — was traditionally made from lichen pigments.

Lichens produce a remarkable range of chemical compounds — acids, pigments, and other substances — that are found nowhere else in nature. These lichen substances or lichen acids serve various purposes: they deter animals from eating the lichen, they protect against UV light, they help break down rock, and they inhibit competing organisms. There are hundreds of such compounds unique to lichens, and they continue to attract scientific interest for potential medicinal and industrial uses.

What makes lichens conceptually important beyond their biology is what they represent: the power of cooperation. Two organisms that are biologically very different — a fungus and a photosynthetic microorganism — fuse their abilities so completely that the result is an entirely new kind of life form, capable of surviving on bare rock in Antarctica, or on the surface of a gravestone for five centuries.

There are over 20,000 described species of lichen worldwide, and they cover roughly 6–8% of Earth's land surface — from tropical rainforest trees to the ice-free rocks of Antarctica. They are quietly, slowly, persistently present almost everywhere on land, often going unnoticed precisely because they look like part of the surface they live on.

When you see that crusty gray or orange patch on an old stone wall or boulder, you are looking at two organisms that found each other, struck an ancient deal, and together made a life in a place where neither could have survived alone.
9794: Something is licit if it is permitted — allowed by law, rules, or accepted standards. If an action or thing falls within what is officially or morally authorized, it is licit.
The Trick That Makes It Click Forever

Here's the most important thing to know: most people have never heard "licit," but almost everyone has heard "illicit" — as in illicit drugs or illicit activity. "Illicit" simply means not licit, i.e., forbidden or unlawful. The prefix "il-" means "not."

So "licit" is the base word that "illicit" was built from. If you know "illicit," you already understand "licit" — it's just the permitted, acceptable side of the line.

Illicit → not allowed. Licit → allowed. That's the whole relationship.

This is where it gets slightly richer, and understanding this will give you a complete picture. "Licit" doesn't only mean legal in the narrow sense of a country's written laws. It refers to permission from whichever authority is relevant in context:

In a legal context, licit means not against the law. Selling alcohol to adults is a licit business in most countries.

In a religious context, licit means in accordance with the religion's rules and norms. In Catholic canon law, for example, a sacrament can be valid (it counts) but still illicit (it was performed in violation of Church regulations). Here, "licit" has nothing to do with civil law — it means properly authorized within that religious framework.

In a moral or philosophical context, licit refers to what is considered ethically permissible, not just legally so.

The word is therefore flexible and context-sensitive. It always means "permitted according to the rules that govern this situation," whether those rules are legal, institutional, or moral.

• The trade in these goods was entirely licit — no laws were broken.
  • She questioned whether the licit use of this drug was as effective as claimed.
  • The government drew a clear line between licit and illicit forms of protest.
  • Even a licit activity can become illicit if carried out in the wrong way or by the wrong person.
  • The sale of tobacco to adults is licit in most jurisdictions, though heavily regulated.

"Licit" and "legal" overlap significantly, but there is a meaningful difference in their reach. "Legal" almost always refers specifically to the law of a state or country. "Licit" is broader — it can extend to moral, religious, or institutional authority. This means something can be legal (not against state law) yet simultaneously illicit within a specific religious or professional framework.

This broader flexibility is exactly why "licit" is useful in formal writing where the writer needs a word that covers permissibility across different types of authority, not just civil law.
Register: When and Where You'll See This Word

"Licit" is a formal word and you will almost never hear it in everyday conversation. People would normally say "legal," "allowed," or "permitted" instead. You'll encounter "licit" mainly in legal or academic writing, philosophy, ethics, religious texts, and formal policy documents.

Interestingly, it's one of those rare words where the negative form — "illicit" — is far more common in everyday use than the positive form "licit" itself. You're much more likely to see "illicit" in a news headline than to see "licit" anywhere at all.
Lawful, legal, permissible, legitimate, authorized, sanctioned, allowable.
Illicit, unlawful, illegal, forbidden, prohibited, unauthorized, impermissible.
Licit means permitted or allowed — by law, moral standards, or relevant rules — and it is simply the opposite of the far more commonly used word "illicit."
9795:
When someone is licking their wounds, it means they are taking time to recover — emotionally, mentally, or physically — after a painful defeat, failure, embarrassment, or setback.

It describes the quiet period a person goes through after something bad has happened to them, where they pull back from the world, feel sorry for themselves, and slowly try to heal and regain their strength and confidence before moving forward again.

Think of it as the human version of retreating to a corner after getting hurt.
The Literal Origin — Where Did It Come From?

The idiom comes directly from the animal kingdom. When animals — dogs, cats, lions, and others — get injured, they literally lick their wounds. This is not random behavior. Animal saliva contains certain enzymes and proteins that have mild antibacterial and healing properties. So licking a wound is the animal's natural, instinctive way of cleaning and soothing an injury.

Humans observed this behavior in animals for thousands of years and eventually borrowed the image to describe a similar kind of behavior in people — not physical licking, of course, but the same idea of quietly tending to your pain before getting back on your feet.

The expression has roots going back to ancient times and appears in various forms across many languages and cultures, which shows just how universal this idea is.
Breaking It Down — Literal vs. Figurative

Literal (Animals)Figurative (Humans)
The woundA physical cut or injuryA defeat, failure, rejection, or humiliation
The lickingCleaning and soothing the wound with salivaRecovering emotionally, reflecting, feeling sad
The purposePhysical healingEmotional and mental healing
The Feeling Behind the Idiom

This idiom carries a very specific emotional flavor. It suggests:

  • Hurt and pain — something genuinely bad happened.
  • Withdrawal — the person has stepped back from the situation.
  • Passivity — they are not yet fighting back or moving forward.
  • A temporary state — it implies they will eventually recover and re-engage, but not yet.

It is not a positive or energetic phrase. It describes a bruised, low-energy period. However, it also isn't completely hopeless — there is a quiet understanding that the person is healing and will eventually get up again.
Everyday Examples to Make It Crystal Clear

Here are examples across different life situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits:

After losing a competition:

"Our team lost the championship game by one point. We're all just licking our wounds this week, but we'll be back stronger next season."

After a business failure:

"His startup failed after two years of hard work. He's been licking his wounds at home and hasn't spoken to anyone about what went wrong yet."

After a breakup:

"She went through a painful breakup last month. She's still licking her wounds — watching movies alone, avoiding social events."

After a public embarrassment:

"The politician made a huge mistake in his speech and got mocked everywhere. He retreated from the public eye to lick his wounds before addressing it."

After a job rejection:

"I didn't get the promotion I worked so hard for. I'm licking my wounds today, but I'll figure out my next move soon."

In every example, you can see the same pattern: something went wrong → the person stepped back → they are quietly recovering.
The Tone — When Do People Use It?

The idiom can be used in a few different tones depending on context:

Sympathetically — when you feel sorry for someone:

"Poor guy. He tried so hard and still lost. Let him lick his wounds in peace."

Matter-of-factly — as a simple observation:

"After the loss, the team went home to lick their wounds before their next match."

Slightly dismissively — when implying someone is overreacting or taking too long to recover:

"Oh, stop licking your wounds and get back out there. One failure won't kill you."

Self-referentially — when you say it about yourself:

"I'm just going to spend the weekend licking my wounds and then start fresh on Monday."
Important Nuance — It Is Always Temporary

A very important thing to understand is that licking one's wounds is always a temporary phase. The idiom doesn't describe someone who has completely given up. It describes someone in the in-between stage — after the hit, but before the comeback.

If you say someone is licking their wounds, it implies:

  • They have been defeated.
  • They are not yet ready to face things again.
  • They will eventually recover and return.

This is what makes it different from saying someone "gave up" or "quit." Licking wounds is about healing, not surrendering permanently.
Grammar — How Is It Used Structurally?

The idiom is a verb phrase, and it changes form depending on who is doing the recovering:

  • I am licking my wounds.
  • He is licking his wounds.
  • She went home to lick her wounds.
  • They spent the week licking their wounds.
  • We need some time to lick our wounds.
  • The team is still licking its wounds after that devastating loss.

The key verb is always "lick" and the object is always the possessive "wounds" matching the subject.
Similar Expressions (Same Idea, Different Words)

These phrases carry a very similar meaning, so knowing them helps you understand the idea more deeply:

  • "Nurse one's wounds" — almost identical in meaning; slightly more gentle in tone.
  • "Retreat and regroup" — pulling back to gather strength before trying again.
  • "Lie low" — staying out of sight after something bad.
  • "Take time to heal" — more literal and straightforward, less colorful.
  • "Dust oneself off" — this is actually the next step after licking wounds; it means getting back up and trying again.
Opposite Expressions

These phrases mean the opposite — bouncing back quickly instead of withdrawing:

  • "Get back on the horse" — immediately trying again after failure.
  • "Shake it off" — not letting the defeat affect you for long.
  • "Bounce back" — recovering quickly and strongly.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

"Licking one's wounds" means quietly recovering from a painful defeat, failure, or setback — stepping back from the world to heal emotionally before finding the strength to move forward again.

That is everything you need to know about this idiom — its meaning, origin, emotional tone, grammar, usage in context, and how it compares to similar and opposite expressions. You now have a complete picture of it.
9796:
A lickspittle is a person who is deeply, embarrassingly eager to please someone powerful — so eager that they lose all dignity doing it. They flatter, agree with, and serve a powerful person not because they genuinely respect them, but because they want something in return: favor, protection, status, money, or simply to avoid being on the wrong side of that person.

In one word: a groveler.

A lickspittle doesn't just admire someone powerful. That would be normal. What makes a lickspittle is a specific, toxic combination of three things:

1. Excessive, fake flattery
A lickspittle constantly praises the powerful person — their ideas, their looks, their decisions — even when that praise is obviously untrue or exaggerated. If the boss makes a terrible decision, the lickspittle calls it brilliant. If the king tells a bad joke, the lickspittle laughs the hardest.

2. Total, spineless agreement
A lickspittle never challenges, contradicts, or disagrees with the person they serve. They simply echo whatever that person says. They have no opinions of their own — or if they do, they hide them completely. Their only job is to nod.

3. A complete surrender of self-respect
This is the defining part. Most people will be polite to their boss, or choose their battles wisely. A lickspittle goes far beyond that — they will humiliate themselves, betray others, or act against their own values just to stay in the powerful person's good graces. There is no line they won't cross to keep that person happy.

The word carries a strong sense of moral disgust. Calling someone a lickspittle is not just describing their behavior — it is condemning them for it.

A lickspittle always exists in relation to someone above them in power. There is always a master and a servant in this picture:

  • A royal courtier who tells the king only what he wants to hear → lickspittle
  • An employee who blames colleagues to protect the boss → lickspittle
  • A politician who publicly defends a leader's every action to stay in their inner circle → lickspittle

The powerful person may or may not be aware of what the lickspittle is doing. Sometimes the powerful person enjoys and encourages it. Sometimes they are being fooled by it.

Crucially, the lickspittle's loyalty is not genuine. It is entirely self-serving. They don't serve the powerful person out of love or true respect. They do it for personal gain. The moment it stops being useful to them, their "loyalty" would vanish.
How It Feels to Observe a Lickspittle

When you watch a lickspittle in action, the feeling is one of second-hand embarrassment and contempt. Their behavior is so over-the-top, so obviously fake, and so undignified that it makes observers uncomfortable. Everyone in the room can see what's happening — everyone except, perhaps, the person being flattered.
How It Differs from Similar Words

There are several words that overlap with lickspittle, but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Yes-man — focuses mainly on the habit of agreeing with everything; less emphasis on the groveling or the disgust
  • Sycophant — the most formal and clinical version of the same idea; means the same thing but sounds more academic and less visceral
  • Toady — very close in meaning; also implies crawling servility, but "lickspittle" is stronger and more colorful
  • Flatterer — only captures one part of it (the false praise); a flatterer might still have dignity, a lickspittle does not

Lickspittle is the most vivid and contemptuous of all these words. It is the one you reach for when you want to express not just what someone does, but how revolting it is.

This is a strong, colorful, and deliberately insulting word. You would use it to express contempt. It is not a neutral description. If you call someone a lickspittle, you are judging them — saying they have sold their dignity cheaply.

It is more common in British English and in literature, history, and political commentary than in casual everyday conversation, but it is immediately understood when used.
A Simple Example to Cement It

Imagine a powerful CEO who is rude, makes poor decisions, and surrounds himself with people who want to protect their jobs. One employee, Marcus, publicly praises every idea the CEO has, laughs at every joke, blames other colleagues when things go wrong to deflect criticism from the CEO, and privately tells the CEO exactly what he wants to hear — even when it is clearly false. Marcus has never once disagreed with the CEO in three years.

Marcus is a lickspittle.

He is not loyal. He is not a friend. He is performing submission in exchange for safety and privilege. And everyone watching finds it both pitiable and disgusting.
A lickspittle is a person who shamelessly flatters, agrees with, and serves someone powerful — not out of genuine respect, but for personal gain — surrendering all dignity and honesty in the process.
9797: Licorice is a plant — and also the name given to several things that come from that plant: its root, the extract made from that root, and the candy flavored with it. Think of the word as having a few connected meanings that all trace back to the same plant.

Licorice is a shrubby plant that grows in parts of Europe and Asia. It has thin leaves and small purple or blue flowers. But the truly important part of this plant is hidden underground — its root.

The licorice root is long, brown on the outside, and yellow on the inside. What makes it remarkable is that it contains a natural compound called glycyrrhizin, which is about 50 times sweeter than sugar. This makes the root taste intensely sweet, with a slightly bitter edge and a flavor somewhat similar to anise (a spice) or fennel.

When people refer to licorice root, they literally mean the dried or raw underground root of this plant, sometimes sold in herbal stores as a stick you can chew on or brew into a tea.

When the licorice root is boiled, concentrated, and dried, it produces a thick, dark, shiny paste or solid block. This is called licorice extract (or licorice root extract). It is very dark — almost black — and has a powerful, sweet, slightly bittersweet flavor.

This extract is used as a flavoring ingredient in:

  • Candies and sweets
  • Cough syrups and throat lozenges (medicines)
  • Chewing tobacco
  • Some alcoholic drinks (like the Italian liqueur sambuca or the French drink pastis)
  • Certain herbal teas

So when you see "licorice" listed as an ingredient, it usually refers to this extract.

The most familiar meaning of "licorice" in everyday life is the candy. Licorice candy is a chewy, soft sweet made using licorice extract as its flavoring. Traditional licorice candy is black in color and has that distinctive sweet-yet-slightly-bitter taste from the extract.

You'll find it shaped in many ways — twisted ropes, coins, wheels, soft pieces, or firm sticks.

Important distinction — black vs. red licorice:
You may have seen "red licorice" or "strawberry licorice" (brands like Twizzlers, for example). Here's the truth: most red licorice does not actually contain licorice extract at all. It is simply a chewy candy in the shape of licorice, but flavored with strawberry, cherry, or other fruit flavors. The only truly "real" licorice is the black kind, flavored with actual licorice extract.

People's reactions to the taste:
Licorice candy is famously polarizing — people tend to either love it or hate it. The flavor is unusual: it is sweet but also has a herbal, anise-like quality that feels very different from most other candies. Those who dislike it often describe it as medicinal, which makes sense because the same extract is used in cough syrups.

For thousands of years — in Chinese medicine, ancient Egyptian medicine, and European herbal traditions — licorice root has been used to treat various ailments. Common uses include:

  • Soothing sore throats and coughs
  • Easing stomach problems (like heartburn or ulcers)
  • Reducing inflammation
  • As a mild laxative

Today, licorice root extract is still found in many over-the-counter throat lozenges and herbal supplements.

However, it is important to know that too much licorice can be harmful. The glycyrrhizin compound in large quantities can raise blood pressure, cause fluid retention, and affect hormone levels. For this reason, some products use "deglycyrrhizinated licorice" (DGL) — licorice with the glycyrrhizin removed — so you get some of the soothing benefits without the risks.

Separate from the plant or candy, "licorice" is also used as a flavor descriptor. When someone says something "tastes like licorice," they mean it has that characteristic sweet, herbal, slightly anise-like taste.

Several other plants and foods share this flavor profile and are sometimes compared to licorice:

  • Anise seed (used in baking and cooking)
  • Star anise (a spice common in Asian cooking)
  • Fennel (a vegetable and spice)
  • Tarragon (an herb)

These are all different plants from licorice, but they contain similar flavor compounds, which is why they smell and taste similar. This often causes confusion — many "licorice-flavored" candies are actually flavored with anise oil, not licorice extract, because anise oil is cheaper and easier to produce.
You may see this word spelled two ways: licorice (used in American English) and liquorice (used in British English). Both refer to exactly the same thing.

Licorice is:

  1. A plant whose root is naturally very sweet and has a distinctive herbal flavor.
  2. The dark, concentrated extract made from that root, used in foods and medicines.
  3. The black candy flavored with that extract — chewy, sweet, and slightly bitter.
  4. An herbal remedy used for centuries to soothe throats, coughs, and digestive issues.
  5. A flavor description for anything that tastes sweet and anise-like.

The key thing to remember: the word always connects back to one source — the root of the licorice plant and its intensely sweet, distinctive flavor.
9798:
Imagine medieval Europe — kings, knights, castles, and sworn oaths of loyalty. Society was built like a pyramid. At the very top sat the king. Below him were powerful nobles. Below them were lesser lords and knights. Everyone owed loyalty, obedience, and service to the person above them in exchange for land and protection. This whole system is called feudalism.

The word liege lives right at the heart of this system. It refers to a person in this chain of loyalty — and here is the interesting part: it can refer to either side of that relationship.

1. The Lord — "My Liege"

A liege can be a sovereign lord — the master, the ruler, the one to whom a person owes their deepest loyalty and obedience.

When a knight kneeled before his king and said "Yes, my liege," he was addressing his lord and master — the person he had sworn to serve above all others. The king, in this context, is the liege.

Think of it as: the one you are completely loyal to.

2. The Subject — "His Lieges"

A liege can also be a loyal subject or vassal — the person giving the loyalty, not the one receiving it.

When a king looked out over his kingdom and spoke of "my lieges," he meant his loyal followers — the people who had sworn their allegiance and service to him. Those devoted subjects are the lieges.

Think of it as: the one who is completely loyal to you.
How Can One Word Mean Both Things?

This sounds confusing, but it makes perfect sense once you understand that liege describes the bond, not just one person in it. It is a word that captures a relationship of supreme, binding loyalty — and both the lord and the servant exist within that same bond. Context always makes it clear which side is being referred to.

This is similar to how the word "partner" can refer to either person in a business partnership — both people are partners, even though they may have different roles.
The Key Quality: It's the Highest Loyalty

This is the razor-sharp detail that separates liege from just any lord-and-servant relationship.

In the feudal world, a person could technically have multiple lords — perhaps he held land from two different nobles. But he could only have one liege lord — the one lord whose claim on his loyalty came first, above all others. The liege relationship was the most sacred, most binding, most unbreakable bond of loyalty a person could have. It wasn't casual service. It was an oath of supreme allegiance.

If two lords ever called the same knight to war on opposite sides, the knight was bound — morally and legally — to fight for his liege lord. The others came second.

RoleWho They AreExample
Liege (lord)The supreme master you serveA king to his knight
Liege (subject)The loyal follower who servesA knight to his king

"Liege" is not a word you'll hear in everyday modern conversation. But you will encounter it in:

  • Historical fiction and fantasy novels — characters address their ruler as "my liege" all the time.
  • Films and TV shows set in medieval or fantasy worlds.
  • Formal, ceremonial, or literary writing where an archaic, noble tone is intended.
  • Humorous or dramatic use — someone might jokingly say "as you wish, my liege" to a bossy friend.

In all these cases, calling someone "my liege" signals one thing clearly: you are my lord, my master, and I serve you with total loyalty.

A liege is either a supreme lord to whom absolute loyalty is owed, or a loyal subject who owes that absolute loyalty — the word describes both sides of the highest, most binding bond of allegiance that existed in feudal society.
9799:
A lien is a legal right that one person or organization holds over someone else's property, as security for a debt or obligation that hasn't been paid yet.

Think of it like this: imagine a lien is a legal "flag" planted on your property. That flag says, "This person is owed money. Until they're paid, this property cannot freely change hands." The property is still yours — you still live in it, use it, and own it — but you cannot fully sell it, transfer it, or in some cases refinance it, without first dealing with that flag.

The person who owes the debt is called the debtor (or lienee), and the person who holds the lien — the one who is owed money — is called the lienholder (or lienor). The property that the lien is placed on is called the collateral.

Say you hire a plumber to fix your pipes. The job costs $5,000, and you agree to pay after the work is done. The plumber finishes the job, but you refuse to pay. In many places, the law allows the plumber to place a mechanic's lien (also called a contractor's lien) on your home. Now, if you try to sell your house, the title search that any buyer's lawyer will run will reveal that lien. You cannot hand over a clean title to the buyer until you've paid the plumber. The lien forces your hand — it turns your property into leverage that protects the plumber's right to be paid.

Liens exist because they give creditors a reliable way to protect themselves. Without liens, a creditor who is owed money would have very few options if the debtor refused to pay — they'd have to sue, go to court, and hope they eventually recover something. A lien cuts through a lot of that uncertainty by attaching the claim directly to something of real value. It says: "Even if you try to ignore me, you can't move this asset without settling with me first."

Liens come into existence in two ways.

A voluntary lien is one you agree to. The most common example in everyday life is a mortgage. When you borrow money from a bank to buy a house, you voluntarily grant the bank a lien on that house. You're essentially saying, "If I don't repay this loan, you have the legal right to take the house." You walked into this arrangement knowingly. A car loan works the same way — the lender holds a lien on your car until the loan is paid off, which is why the lender's name may appear on your car's title.

An involuntary lien is imposed on you without your agreement, usually because you failed to fulfill an obligation. The plumber example above is one. A tax lien is another — if you don't pay your taxes, the government can place a lien on your property, your bank accounts, and other assets without needing your permission. A judgment lien arises when someone sues you in court and wins — the court's judgment can automatically become a lien on your property.
The Most Common Types of Liens

Mortgage lien: The most familiar lien. A bank lends you money to buy real estate and holds a lien on that property until the loan is fully repaid. If you stop paying, the bank can foreclose — meaning they can legally force a sale of the property to recover what they're owed.

Tax lien: Placed by a government authority (federal, state, or local) when taxes go unpaid. Tax liens are considered extremely serious because the government is treated as a high-priority creditor. A federal tax lien in the United States, for example, can attach to virtually all of your property and assets.

Mechanic's lien (or contractor's lien): Used by contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, and workers who provided labor or materials for a construction or repair project but were not paid. It attaches to the real estate on which the work was done.

Judgment lien: When a court rules that you owe someone money and you don't pay voluntarily, the winning party can often convert that court judgment into a lien on your real property. This ensures they'll eventually be paid when you sell or refinance.

Artisan's lien: A craftsman or repair person (a jeweler, mechanic, tailor) who does work on your personal property can sometimes hold onto that property until you pay. A mechanic who repairs your car but isn't paid can, in many jurisdictions, keep the car under an artisan's lien.
Priority: When There Are Multiple Liens

A single piece of property can have more than one lien on it. When that happens, the question of who gets paid first becomes important — and this is decided by lien priority.

Generally, the rule is "first in time, first in right" — whoever recorded their lien first has the highest priority. But there are exceptions. Tax liens, for example, often leap to the front of the line regardless of when they were recorded, because the law treats government tax claims as especially important. A first mortgage (the original home loan) almost always has priority over a second mortgage or a home equity line of credit.

Priority matters enormously when a property is sold in foreclosure. If the sale doesn't generate enough money to pay everyone, creditors with lower-priority liens may get little or nothing.

A lien doesn't last forever. Once the underlying debt or obligation is fully paid, the lienholder is required to file a lien release (sometimes called a satisfaction of lien or discharge of lien) with the appropriate authority — typically the county recorder or land registry office. This removes the flag from the property and gives the debtor a clean title.

If a lienholder refuses to release a lien after being paid, the debtor can generally go to court to force the release. Conversely, if a lien was filed incorrectly or without legal basis, the property owner can challenge it and have it removed.

It's worth being clear about what a lien is not:

A lien is not the same as ownership. The lienholder does not own your property. They simply have a legal claim attached to it.

A lien is not the same as repossession. Holding a lien doesn't mean the creditor can immediately walk up and take your stuff. There's a legal process that must be followed — usually a notice, a waiting period, and sometimes court involvement — before any creditor can act on a lien.

A lien is not a loan. A lien is the security instrument that backs a loan. The loan is the debt; the lien is the legal protection the lender puts in place to secure that debt.

A lien is a tool that balances two interests: it protects creditors who are owed money, and it does so in a way that is legally transparent — liens are recorded in public records, so anyone who searches (like a potential buyer or new lender) can see them before making a decision. This transparency is what makes the whole system trustworthy. You always know what you're getting into when you buy a property or lend money against one, because the liens are visible.

In short: a lien is a legal claim on someone's property, held by a creditor, that survives until the underlying debt is settled. It doesn't take the property away from you, but it chains the property to the obligation — and that chain doesn't break until the debt does.
